content: 1. HIV Care and Treatment: In some countries, nurses play a critical role in providing HIV care and treatment. These nurses may include registered nurses, clinical nurse specialists, licensed nurses, auxiliary nurses, dental nurses, and primary care nurses, all of whom are trained in basic nursing skills or authorized to practice as nurses. 2. People-Centered Care: This approach focuses on organizing healthcare around the specific health needs and expectations of individuals and communities, rather than centering care solely on diseases. 3. Point-of-Care Testing: This type of testing is performed at the location where clinical care is provided. Results are returned to the patient or caregiver on the same day as sample collection, enabling timely clinical decision-making. 4. Pretreatment Drug Resistance: 5. PrEP involves the use of ARV drugs by individuals who are not infected with HIV to prevent acquiring the virus. 6. Rapid ART Initiation: This refers to starting ART within seven days of an HIV diagnosis. 7. Retention in Care: 8. Substantial Risk of HIV Infection: This is provisionally defined as an HIV incidence rate greater than 3 per 100 person-years in the absence of PrEP. Individual risk varies within groups at substantial risk based on behaviors and characteristics of sexual partners. People at substantial risk are present in most countries and may include key and vulnerable populations, as well as others not explicitly identified as such. 9. Task Sharing: This involves redistributing tasks among healthcare workers with varying levels of training, such as shifting responsibilities from highly trained professionals to lay providers with shorter training periods. 10. Viral Suppression: This is achieved when the viral load in an individual is undetectable, defined as less than 50 copies per milliliter. 11. Virological Failure: This occurs when a person on ART has a persistently detectable viral load exceeding 1,000 copies per milliliter after at least six months of treatment. 12. Vulnerable Populations: These groups are at increased risk of HIV infection due to specific situations or contexts, such as infants, children, adolescents (including adolescent girls in sub-Saharan Africa), orphans, people with disabilities, and migrant or mobile workers. They may face social and legal barriers to accessing HIV prevention and treatment. Vulnerability varies across countries and epidemics, and each country should define its specific vulnerable populations based on epidemiological and social contexts. 13. Dosages of ARV Drugs for Adults and Adolescents: Specific dosages for various ARV drug classes, such as nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), nucleotide reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NtRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), protease inhibitors (PIs), and integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs), are outlined. Adjustments are recommended for individuals receiving tuberculosis (TB) therapy, particularly in the presence of rifampicin or rifabutin. 14. Weight-Based Dosing for Infants and Children: ARV drug formulations for infants and children are prescribed based on weight bands rather than per kilogram or body surface area. Simplified dosing schedules are designed to minimize overor under-dosing. Neonates and preterm infants require special consideration due to immature renal and hepatic functions, and dosing for this group remains challenging due to limited pharmacokinetic data. 15. Preferred ARV Formulations for Children: Dispersible tablets or granules are preferred over oral liquids or syrups, except for neonatal treatment. Children should transition to solid oral dosage forms as soon as possible. Fixed-dose combinations are recommended when available, and scored tablets are preferred for accurate dosing. 16. Special Considerations for Neonates and Preterm Infants: Neonates younger than two weeks and preterm infants require careful management due to rapid growth and organ maturation. Certain ARV drugs, such as lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), should not be used in neonates younger than two weeks or preterm infants until they reach 42 weeks of gestational age. 17. Updates on ARV Dosing Guidelines: Recent updates include the inclusion of integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) like dolutegravir (DTG) in preferred regimens for children. Simplified dosing schedules and new formulations, such as DTG dispersible tablets, have been approved for children as young as four weeks old and weighing at least 3 kg. Ongoing research aims to refine dosing for younger and smaller children. 18. National Program Considerations: National recommendations should consider the availability and regulatory status of specific formulations. 19. Research and Development: Efforts are ongoing to develop optimal ARV formulations and establish dosing guidance for neonates, infants, and young children. Updated recommendations will be provided as new evidence and formulations become available. This summary reflects the latest guidelines and recommendations for HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and care delivery, with a focus on ensuring effective and safe management for all populations, including vulnerable groups and children.
